On 24 February 2022 Russia launched a full invasion of Ukraine, starting the largest and deadliest war in Europe since the Second World War. It was a major escalation of a war that began in 2014, when Russia seized Crimea and backed armed separatists in the Donbas.

Russian columns drove on Kyiv from the north, but Ukrainian forces held them off. Ukraine retook ground around Kharkiv and Kherson in late 2022. After that the front hardened into trenches, minefields and drone warfare across the east and south, with Russia holding about a fifth of the country.

President Vladimir Putin cast the war as a stand against the West. Ukraine under Volodymyr Zelenskyy fought for its survival as a state, with weapons and money from the United States and Europe. Hundreds of thousands of soldiers have been killed or wounded, and the Ukrainian refugee crisis sent 6 to 7 million people abroad.

The war pushed Finland and Sweden into NATO and cut Europe off from most Russian gas. Both sides draw on a shared past that runs back to Kievan Rus and through the breakup of the Soviet Union in 1991.
